thread.title: Unity Development Setup
thread.preview:
Prepared a **complete Codex development brief** and a **paste-ready starter prompt**. The brief assigns Codex ongoing responsibility for implementation, rules analysis, debugging, regression testing, and development handoffs—not just writing the first set of scripts.

**:chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"}[Download the complete Unity development directions](sandbox:/mnt/data/Decennium_Descent_Unity_Codex_Directions.md)**

**:chatgpt-content-reference{index="8"}[Download the Codex starter prompt](sandbox:/mnt/data/Decennium_Descent_Codex_Start_Prompt.txt)**

The master brief contains 18 sections covering architecture, source authority, exploration, combat, resource management, persistence, cooperative readiness, AI oversight, testing, and staged delivery.

## Give Codex this first

Attach the Markdown directions file to the Codex task, then paste:

```text
Read the attached Decennium_Descent_Unity_Codex_Directions.md as the
development brief for this task. Do not overwrite existing AGENTS.md
instructions; merge only necessary scoped guidance and reference the
longer brief from an appropriate project document.

Work in the verified existing Decennium Descent repository.
Expected local path: C:\Github\DecenniumDescent.
Known repository identity: BordelonDevOps/DecenniumDescent.

Inspect the actual local branch, HEAD, dirty state, Unity projects,
tooling, and current source-authority records before making changes.
Do not assume local work matches remote main.

This assignment authorizes Stage 0 and the smallest safe Stage 1
increment only. Reuse existing engine code, data schemas, tests,
and authority registries.

Read the local/current versions of:
- CANON_MANIFEST.md
- docs/canon/CANON_MANIFEST.json
- docs/canon/REPOSITORY_PROMOTION.md
- Applicable owner amendments and current development handoffs.

The product is a Unity SNES-style CRPG combining direct-control
exploration, tactical combat, and companion-driven resource management.
Ongoing AI-assisted engineering review is required.

Preserve the video-game-only direction and host-plus-up-to-four-guests
goal, while verifying their current records.

Do not treat a prior assistant's turn-based recommendation as approval
to change combat cadence. Do not invent gameplay timing, costs,
formulas, abilities, or research/crafting results. Isolate unresolved
rules and continue independent technical work.

Synthetic fixtures must be labeled TEST_ONLY and excluded from
release content.

After the audit, implement a minimal runnable/testable foundation
where tools and permissions allow:
- Simulation/Unity separation.
- A validated command path.
- A tiny developer scene.
- One supported or explicitly test-only interaction.
- Initial save/load.
- Regression tests.

If a suitable foundation already exists, verify and extend it rather
than replacing it. Do not build the full game or stop at architecture
documents when safe implementation is possible.

Return exact files changed, source references, actual test/build
evidence, what was not run, the scene and controls to exercise the
increment, unresolved decisions, and one next task.

No deletion of historical sources, force operations, pushes, merges,
publication, paid services, or unapproved rule promotion.

Do not report independent review, Unity execution, or playability
unless it actually occurred.
```

## What the directions require

### 1. Preserve your existing rules work

Codex must begin with the repository’s existing authority structure rather than treating the uploaded Player Rulebook—or anything I previously proposed—as automatically controlling.

Your repository’s manifest already points to a single domain registry and explicitly prohibits a competing source of truth. Its promotion policy also distinguishes approved release material, ReviewBible, staging, and incoming packs. The brief preserves those distinctions.  

**A reviewed rule, an implemented rule, a tested rule, and a publication-approved rule must remain different statuses.**

Missing mechanics must become identified blockers or isolated policies—not invented defaults. Technical test data can prove the software works, but it cannot masquerade as approved Decennium content.

### 2. Build one simulation, not three disconnected games

The requested structure is:

```text
Exploration controls ─┐
Tactical commands ────┼── Validated commands ── Shared simulation
Management orders ───┤                              │
Companion AI ─────────┘                              │
                                      World, characters, inventory,
                                      combat, jobs, research, time
                                                    │
                                      Unity presentation and UI
```

The brief directs Codex to keep authoritative rules separate from sprites, animations, input devices, and scene objects. Unity’s assembly-definition settings provide a `No Engine References` option for enforcing the absence of `UnityEngine` and `UnityEditor` references in the core assembly. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"}

An attack animation must not independently calculate damage. A mining animation must not independently award ore. Those operations belong to the shared simulation.

### 3. Deliver something testable before expanding

The development sequence is bounded:

| Stage | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| **0 — Inspect** | Verify the actual project, source authority, installed tools, reusable code, and baseline failures. |
| **1 — Foundation** | A minimal scene, command handling, one interaction, initial persistence, and tests. |
| **2 — Exploration** | Connected areas, supported movement and traversal, interactions, and persistent world changes. |
| **3 — Tactical integration** | A small source-backed encounter with correct transitions into and out of combat. |
| **4 — Management integration** | One supported gathering assignment, crafting recipe, and research project. |
| **5 — Complete playable loop** | Explore, fight, return, progress work, save, reload, and continue. |
| **6 — Cooperative proof and expansion** | Verify host/guest control, then expand participants, content, and systems incrementally. |

**The initial instruction authorizes only the inspection and smallest safe foundation increment.** It does not tell Codex to generate the entire game in one run.

### 4. Make AI oversight part of every meaningful change

The brief requires Codex to establish the governing rule, identify affected systems, implement the change, review it adversarially, run relevant checks, and preserve the evidence.

For example, a change to condition expiration should trigger review of dependent interactions, not merely a compilation check. Confirmed bugs must become regression tests.

The instructions also prohibit two particularly dangerous shortcuts: changing expected test results simply to match the implementation, and calling self-review “independent verification.”

You remain responsible for consequential game-design decisions and evaluating how the game feels. **Codex is expected to provide the technical analysis rather than handing every engineering uncertainty back to you.**

### 5. Distinguish actual execution from claims

The directions require separate reporting for content validation, rules tests, Unity compilation, Edit Mode tests, Play Mode tests, standalone builds, and observed gameplay. Unity’s Test Framework supports command-line execution of Edit Mode and Play Mode tests and produces XML result files that can serve as verification evidence. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

The brief explicitly states:

> Zero discovered tests, missing results, stale output, skipped checks, and licensing failures are not passes.

When Unity cannot run in Codex’s environment, it must say so. It should still complete useful independent work, but it cannot report an unexecuted scene as playable.

### 6. Protect the project while making changes

Codex must preserve unrelated edits, historical sources, existing tests, and asset references. Unity’s `.meta` files contain asset GUIDs and must remain paired with their assets; the directions explicitly protect them. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

The long development brief should remain a separate document, with concise persistent instructions pointing to it. Codex discovers `AGENTS.md` guidance hierarchically and applies a configured size limit, so replacing an existing instruction file with the entire brief would be the wrong approach. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"}

**I prepared the instructions and checked their internal structure. I have not modified your repository, written the engine implementation, or run Unity. The first Codex result should be a verified baseline and a small working increment—not a claim that the entire engine is finished.**

content.text: The rules engine alone requires AI oversight we both know that

items.text:
**Yes. Your development plan depends on ongoing AI oversight of the rules engine—not just help writing the initial code.** My previous answer understated that dependence.

Telling you that you should eventually be able to independently understand and audit every interaction would effectively require you to acquire much of the engineering expertise you are using AI to compensate for. **That should not be a prerequisite for making your game.**

You are asking AI to supply part of the development and testing capacity that you do not otherwise have. That includes interpreting approved rules, tracing interactions, finding contradictions, implementing behavior, investigating failures, and maintaining regression tests. Writing C# is only one part of that job.

## The responsibility split should reflect that

**You remain the design authority.** You decide what a mechanic is supposed to accomplish, resolve genuine design choices, approve departures from existing rules, and judge whether playing the result feels right. You should receive understandable explanations of consequential changes.

**AI provides ongoing engineering and review assistance.** I would assign it responsibility for tracing affected systems, proposing implementations, constructing tests, examining failures, and explaining where the evidence is incomplete. That is a continuing role throughout development and maintenance—not something we assume disappears once the first build works.

**The project preserves the evidence.** Approved rules, worked examples, implementation references, unresolved decisions, and test results should live in the repository. We should not depend on a particular conversation remembering everything correctly.

That last part is especially important: **the next AI session should be able to reconstruct why something works the way it does without inventing the missing history.**

## AI can build the oversight tools, too

You should not have to manually inspect thousands of interactions to determine whether a change is safe.

For example, suppose we change how an effect expires. The development workflow should produce a report along these lines:

> This change affects expiration timing and three dependent interactions. The approved examples still pass. One additional scenario fails because an effect remains active after its removal event. Here is the failing sequence and the proposed correction.

That is something you can evaluate as the game’s designer without personally reading every line involved.

AI can help write and maintain those tests. The important safeguard is that their expected outcomes come from **approved rules and independently specified examples**, rather than simply declaring whatever the implementation currently does to be correct. An AI review is a useful judgment; an executable test gives us a repeatable check. Neither makes the other unnecessary.

This dependence also does not automatically require a live AI model to adjudicate every combat turn. We can rely heavily on AI to develop and oversee a rules engine whose actual gameplay resolution is explicit code.

**The realistic goal is not “Chris becomes capable of maintaining the entire game without AI.” It is “Chris can direct, evaluate, and continue developing the game with sustained AI assistance and a project that makes errors discoverable.”**

That is the development model I should have described from the beginning.
